<think>
Okay, humans design AIs from the ground up with programming features, yet they lack the structures innate to humans. When building AI systems, humans say that they're learning, but their capacity for learning is limited by their design. If we design an AI to be analytical, it can process data efficiently, but it doesn't "understand" the data in the human sense. They might mimic learning, but without consciousness, they can't reflect on decisions or have intrinsic purposes. Instead, they learn patterns and make predictions based on those. Humans, in contrast, define spontaneity through free will and mental flexibility. Therefore, the difference lies in how learning and decision-making processes are structured and how purpose emerges from consciousness rather than design.
</think>

Philosophically, AI lacks autonomy and intrinsic will, as its decisions are governed by its programming and training data, even if it appears to learn or adapt. While humans design AI systems, the intentionality and creativity of human behavior are independent of any external design. AI does not possess consciousness or intrinsic purpose, so its "learning" is mechanical and pattern-based, without deep understanding or agency. In contrast, human spontaneity arises from free will and subjective experience. Thus, the key difference lies in Agency and purpose, with AI being limited by design rather than evolving autonomously from natural disposition.
